extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and patent applicants/practitioners who respond to eligibility rejections)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating patent claims under 35 U.S.C. 101 (the Alice/Mayo framework), including when to use a streamlined analysis, how to identify judicial exceptions, and how to formulate and support eligibility rejections. Covers concepts such as insignificant extra-solution activity, field-of-use limitations, and improvements to technology or computer functionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Insignificant extra-solution activity
rubrics_metrics.description: For claim limitations that add insignificant extra-solution activity to the judicial exception (e.g., mere data gathering in conjunction with a law of nature or abstract idea), examiners should explain in an eligibility rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and guidance: Some cases have identified insignificant computer implementation as an example of insignificant extra-solution activity (Fort Props.; Bancorp Servs.). Examiners should explain why adding a final step of storing data to a process that only recites computing the area of a space (a mathematical relationship) does not add a meaningful limitation to the process of computing the area. See MPEP § 2106.05(f) for more information. When such limitations are present, explain in the rejection why they fail to meaningfully limit the judicial exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Field of use / Technological environment limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Limitations that amount to merely indicating a field of use or technological environment in which to apply a judicial exception do not amount to significantly more than the exception itself, and cannot integrate a judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authoritative examples: Parker v. Flook (limiting a formula to petrochemical/oil-refining was token), Diamond v. Diehr (contrast: specific limitations acting in concert provided eligibility), Affinity Labs (limiting abstract idea to cellular telephones was insufficient). Court-cited examples (i–x) include drug administration limited to a patient population (Mayo), hedging participants limited to commodity providers/consumers (Bilski), limiting C=2πr to wheel circumference (Flook), specifying execution on a generic computer or the Internet (FairWarning; Ultramercial), limiting to power-grid data (Electric Power Group), and others. Examiners should consider 'technological environment' and 'field of use' interchangeable for eligibility analysis and be mindful of overlap with insignificant extra-solution activity (see MPEP § 2106.05(g)). For claim limitations that generally link the judicial exception to a particular technological environment, explain in the rejection why they do not meaningfully limit the claim (e.g., employing generic computer functions to execute an abstract idea does not add significantly more).

rubrics_metrics.name: Streamlined analysis (Pathway A) — use and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners may use a streamlined eligibility analysis (Pathway A) when the eligibility of the claim is self-evident (e.g., because the claim clearly improves a technology or computer functionality).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key points: The streamlined analysis may be used for efficiency but should not be used when there is doubt as to whether the applicant is effectively seeking coverage for a judicial exception — then the full Alice/Mayo test should be conducted. The results of the streamlined analysis will always be the same as the full analysis; it is not a way to avoid a finding of ineligibility that would occur under the full test. If eligibility is self-evident when viewed as a whole (e.g., clear improvement to technology/computer functionality), the claim is eligible at Pathway A. In practice, use of Pathway A may be reflected by absence of an eligibility rejection or clarifying remarks in the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility is self-evident — when to apply
rubrics_metrics.description: A streamlined eligibility analysis can be used for a claim that may or may not recite a judicial exception but, when viewed as a whole, clearly does not seek to tie up any judicial exception such that others cannot practice it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative situations: claims to complex manufactured industrial products or processes that recite meaningful limitations along with a judicial exception (e.g., a robotic arm assembly with a control system using mathematical relationships), nature-based products that clearly do not attempt to tie up the nature-based product (e.g., artificial hip prosthesis coated with a naturally occurring mineral), and claims that merely include ancillary nature-based components (e.g., cellphone with an electrical contact made of gold). If a claim is a 'close call' on whether it improves technology or computer functionality, perform full eligibility analysis (see BASCOM example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Clear improvement to technology or to computer functionality
rubrics_metrics.description: Some improvements to technology or to computer functionality are not abstract when appropriately claimed, and thus claims to such improvements do not always need to undergo the full eligibility analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case guidance: Enfish (self‑referential table for a computer database held eligible), McRO (automatic lip synchronization and facial expression animation found eligible as an improvement). If claims clearly improve computer-related technology or other technologies/technological processes, eligibility may be self-evident (Pathway A) or they may be found not directed to an abstract idea at Step 2A (Pathway B). When the claims present a close call (e.g., BASCOM), proceed to the full Alice/Mayo analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejections must be based on substantive law and the record as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: Eligibility rejections must be based on failure to comply with the substantive law under 35 U.S.C. 101 as interpreted by judicial precedent. Examiners should review the record as a whole before reaching a conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examination should consider the specification, claims, prosecution history, and relevant case law precedent or prior art. Examination of eligibility should be claim‑by‑claim because dependent claims may add limitations that change eligibility. Examination guidance, training, and examples do not themselves serve as a basis for a rejection. Examiners must set forth a prima facie case of ineligibility when concluding a claim is more likely than not ineligible, explaining why clearly and specifically so applicant can respond.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong One — Identify the judicial exception recited in the claim
rubrics_metrics.description: A subject matter eligibility rejection should point to the specific claim limitation(s) that recite the judicial exception and explain why those limitations set forth or describe a judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When the claim describes but does not expressly set forth the judicial exception, explain what subject matter those limitations describe and why the described subject matter is a judicial exception. For abstract ideas, identify the abstract idea as recited in the claim and explain why it falls within the groupings of abstract ideas (mathematical concepts, mental processes, or certain methods of organizing human activity) enumerated in MPEP § 2106.04(a)(2). See MPEP § 2106.04 for more information relevant to Step 2A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2A Prong Two — Identify additional elements and evaluate integration into a practical application
rubrics_metrics.description: For Prong Two, the rejection should identify any additional elements (specifically point to claim features/limitations/steps) recited in the claim beyond the identified judicial exception and evaluate whether those elements integrate the judicial exception into a practical application.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must explain that either 1) there are no additional elements in the claim; or 2) the claim as a whole, looking at the additional elements individually and in combination, does not integrate the judicial exception into a practical application using the considerations set forth in MPEP §§ 2106.04(d), 2106.05(a)-(c) and (e)-(h). Examiners should give weight to all claimed additional elements in Prong Two, even if those elements represent well‑understood, routine, conventional activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Step 2B — Explain why additional elements do not amount to significantly more (inventive concept)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Step 2B, the rejection should explain why the additional elements, taken individually and in combination, do not result in the claim, as a whole, amounting to significantly more than the identified judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the examiner concludes certain claim elements recite well‑understood, routine, conventional activities in the relevant field, the examiner must expressly support the rejection in writing with one of the four options specified in Subsection III. See MPEP §§ 2106.05 et seq. for guidance on searching for an inventive concept and applying Step 2B.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formulating an Office action rejection — required content and adequacy
rubrics_metrics.description: When making a 35 U.S.C. 101 rejection, the Office action must provide an explanation as to why each claim is unpatentable that is sufficiently clear and specific to provide applicant sufficient notice and enable effective response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rejection should provide an explanation for each part of the Step 2 analysis (Prong One, Prong Two, and Step 2B) and specifically point to claim elements and explain the reasons for the examiner's conclusions. See MPEP § 2106.07(a) for details. Under the prima facie concept, the initial burden is on the examiner to explain ineligibility clearly and specifically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compact prosecution and consideration of other patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 is made, a complete examination should be made for every claim under each of the other patentability requirements (35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112, and issues of utility, inventorship, double patenting).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should state all non‑cumulative reasons and bases for rejecting claims in the first Office action. Thus, include all applicable rejections (e.g., anticipation, obviousness, written description, enablement, utility, inventorship, double patenting) even if a 101 rejection is also made.
